    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the manufacturer to scrape the websites of Meta Business account people.

    On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    In a recent development, meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

    In a recent development, “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    It has been revealed that since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For many people, searching the web means opening Google. It’s a familiar place to research a purchase, check a fact, or catch up on the news and that reach shows in the numbers with Google accounting for 91.04% of worldwide search engine referrals according to Statcounter in October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that but the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job. Think about the last time you needed an image you could reuse, a webpage that had disappeared, or a more private way to search. Those are different problems, and a single search box is not always the easiest way to solve them.

    That is where alternatives earn their place. Some give you more control over privacy and rankings, whilst others bring together sources in a conversation, search a specialist collection, or help you explore the content people use in another country. For marketers, those differences also explain why visibility beyond Google involves more than submitting a website to another engine.

    Sources indicate that you don’t have to give up Google to find out what you might be missing. We collated 21 alternative search engines and tools worth trying, whether you’re looking for a better answer or a new way for customers to find your business.

    About the Usage Figures: Entries are ordered within each section by estimated monthly visits to the named website or subdomain. The October 2026 figures are not unique users, search queries, or app activity. Statcounter percentages shown separately measure search referral share, not visits.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 6 billion to chatgpt.com, October 2026. This covers the ChatGPT website, not Search alone.

    ChatGPT is useful when your question needs a conversation rather than a fresh set of keywords each time. You can ask it to compare two approaches, explain an unfamiliar term, and then look for recent evidence without starting over. Its advantage is keeping the context of that investigation together.

    Recent findings suggest that openAI’s search documentation indicates it can retrieve current web information and link to sources. Search is available on free and paid prepares, including for people who are not signed in, although usage limits apply. ChatGPT may search automatically, or you can select Search from its tools.

    It has been revealed that use it to work through a question, then open the citations to check the answer. It can misread a source or miss a qualification, and its use of other search providers means it is not simply a separate, independent web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 88.3 million to perplexity.ai, October 2026.

    Perplexity puts source-backed answers at the center of the search experience. Its research-oriented approach is useful when you want an overview of a subject and a trail of sources to investigate, rather than opening a long list of results before finding the main points.

    It has been revealed that its Pro Search process can conduct multiple searches and bring findings together, with follow-up questions keeping the research in context. Depending on your proposal, you can narrow the work to areas such as academic or financial sources. Access and limits vary by tier.

    The benefit is a faster route into a topic, not a substitute for reading the evidence. Check that each citation supports the statement beside it because AI answers can still contain hallucinations even when links are present.

    Sources indicate that why SEO Experts Should Care: Perplexity can be useful even if it sends less traffic than Google. In his post on why marketers should care about Perplexity, Dennis Goedegebuure argues that it is a low-cost test bench for AI search. Try the research questions your customers ask, inspect which pages get cited, and check how your brand and recently updated facts appear. For B2B marketers, that means testing visibility during product research, rather than judging the opportunity solely by overall visit totals.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.7 billion to bing.com, October 2026.

    Industry observers note that bing is a full-service alternative for everyday web, image, video, and news searches. One concrete reason to try it is Visual Search: when you have a picture of a product, plant, or object but do not know its name, you can start with the image instead of guessing keywords.

    Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s visual search tools can find related images and shopping options, identify objects, and extract or translate text from a picture. Conventional results remain available alongside AI-assisted tools, so an answer does not have to be the end of your search.

    According to recent reports, search Engine Journal covered Bing’s search updates in December 2024, including work on faster, more precise results. Try the same image or video query on Bing and Google to see which makes the next step easier for you; that is more useful than assuming one wins every search.

    Where available, Bing’s Copilot Search adds AI-generated summaries with source citations and suggested follow-up topics, so you can explore a question without starting from scratch.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 751 million to search.yahoo.com, October 2026.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 2.54% in the U.S., October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Yahoo Search makes the most sense if you already use Yahoo for news, finance, or other daily information. Its value is the connection between search and that wider content ecosystem, rather than a completely different index of the web.

    Yahoo introduced Scout in January 2026 as an AI answer engine combining open-web information with Yahoo content and data. The U.S. beta launch named Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft’s Bing grounding API as parts of the system.

    Sources indicate that that gives Yahoo customers a way to move from a headline or financial topic into a sourced explanation. You can still browse traditional search results, and you should follow Scout’s source links when an answer matters. The launch’s audience figures cover Yahoo’s broader services, not people using Scout alone.

    According to recent reports, at Search Engine Journal, Yahoo accounts for about 0.2% of our traffic. It’s a small share, but it still brings a few thousand visits in a month and for a different business, even that smaller stream of visitors could include a potential customer or lead to a sale.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.7 billion to baidu.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    It has been revealed that search Engine Referral Share: 49% in China, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Baidu matters when your research or marketing is aimed at Chinese-language audiences. Its value is not simply in translating an English query, but it offers a view of Chinese-language search and a connected set of local content services.

    Recent findings suggest that alongside web results, its homepage links to maps, images, video, the Baike encyclopedia, Zhidao questions and answers, and Wenku documents. Those services give you distinct places to investigate how a topic, product, or brand is described. Use the terminology that local sources use rather than assuming an English search will surface the same material.

    For marketers, the search referral share is a reason to investigate Baidu separately, not proof that it will send a particular site traffic. Distinguish content hosted inside Baidu’s services from results linking to external publishers, and assess the original source.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.5 billion to naver.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 42.25% in South Korea, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Naver is useful for Korean-language research because its search experience brings together more than external webpages. Naver’s search overview describes results across news, maps, cafés, blogs, images, video, and other categories.

    That mix gives you a route into local experiences and community content as well as conventional reporting. Its community services include Naver Blog, interest-based Café communities, and Knowledge iN questions and answers. If you are researching a Korean product or audience, those are different sources to explore from an English-language web-results page.

    It has been revealed that for website owners, Naver Search Advisor is the official starting point for webmaster tools. Keep visits to an external website separate from engagement with a blog or other content hosted inside Naver.

    Recent findings suggest that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 162.2 million to yandex.com, October 2026. This covers the international website, not total use across all Yandex domains.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 70.22% in Russia, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    It has been revealed that yandex is worth checking when you need Russian-language sources or are researching visibility in Russia. Its large share of measured referrals there gives it a different role from a small global alternative – it is an important regional search environment in its own right.

    Use it to compare which local publishers and pages appear for the terminology your audience actually uses. Its international homepage also presents an AI search option, but the practical reason to investigate it is the regional results and audience context, not simply another chatbot interface.

    SEJ’s Yandex guide provides background for marketers. The 2023 data leak is a separate historical event, not a verified description of today’s ranking system. The search referral share above describes referrals, not the percentage of Russian people using Yandex.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 16.5 million to sogou.com, October 2026.

    Sogou offers another route into Chinese-language information, with a more specific reason to try it rather than simply comparing general web results – its WeChat search is a destination for discovering public accounts and articles from that ecosystem.

    That is useful when the material you need was published as a WeChat article rather than an ordinary standalone webpage. Search in the relevant Chinese terminology and distinguish those public articles from results in Sogou’s general web search.

    In a recent development, this is not access to private messages or every piece of content in WeChat. As with other platform-specific searches, check the account, publication date, and original article before using a result as evidence.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 698.8 million to search.brave.com, October 2026.

    Brave Search combines an independent web index with tools for changing how results are ranked. It is worth trying if you want both an alternative to Google or Bing’s underlying results and more say over which sources rise to the top.

    Its search help describes Goggles, which apply alternative ranking or filtering rules. Brave also describes domain-level ranking controls and an AI answer experience on its about page. Those controls give you something more specific to experiment with than a different-looking results page.

    Industry observers note that SEJ reported Brave’s Bing separation in 2023. You can use Brave Search in another browser, so testing its index does not require adopting Brave’s browser, wallet, VPN, or other products.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 681.9 million to duckduckgo.com, October 2026.

    DuckDuckGo is a straightforward choice if you want everyday search without a personal search-history profile. You can use its search website in your existing browser, so the switch does not require changing your whole browsing setup.

    Recent findings suggest that privacy and index independence are different benefits, however. DuckDuckGo’s source documentation claims traditional links and images largely come from Bing, supplemented by specialist sources, its own crawler, and its own indexes. Choose it for that privacy model, not on the assumption that every result comes from a separate web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 57.6 million to startpage.com, October 2026.

    Startpage is for people who want results from major search providers without dealing with those providers directly. It acts as a privacy intermediary, submitting your query on your behalf and returning the results to you.

    According to recent reports, its partner explanation identifies both Google and Microsoft Bing. Startpage says it does not share personal information with them, and that those providers see Startpage rather than the person making the request.

    Industry observers note that that is the distinction from an independent-index engine: Startpage changes the relationship between you and the search provider, not necessarily the underlying collection of pages. It is worth trying if you like familiar results but want a different privacy arrangement; it is not a way to avoid Google’s infrastructure altogether.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.6 million to kagi.com, October 2026.

    Its Lenses let you narrow searches to selected websites or categories such as forums, academic sources, or PDFs. Kagi’s source documentation describes its own indexes alongside major and specialist providers, with an emphasis on surfacing independent and noncommercial content. It is not powered solely by its Teclis index.

    It has been revealed that as of November 2026, its monthly individual plans include Starter at $5 plus tax for 300 searches and Professional at $10 plus tax for unlimited searches. Annual billing has different terms. If you search heavily and want persistent control over sources, those features are the reason to consider paying.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 219 million to ecosia.org, October 2026.

    Ecosia lets you put the revenue from an everyday habit toward climate work. It says all of its profits go to climate action, with the majority funding tree-planting projects. That is its central reason to exist: changing who benefits financially from search.

    The organization publishes monthly financial reports, so you can look beyond the tree counter to see how money is spent. Its provider documentation lists Bing, Google, and European Search Perspective, or EUSP; the mix depends on factors including region, device, and permissions.

    Recent findings suggest that this makes Ecosia a funding-model choice, not a promise that every query uses a wholly separate index. If you want to support its mission while keeping familiar web search, it is a low-friction option to try. You can check the provider through the information control beside a result.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 451,800 to karmasearch.org, October 2026.

    KARMA applies the search-funded nonprofit model to animal welfare and biodiversity. Its distinction from a broader climate-focused service is the cause: helping fund organizations working on wildlife, habitats, and animal protection.

    The organization’s explanation says sponsored search links generate revenue for its nonprofit partners. Its site lists partners including Re:wild, Humane World for Animals, and iNaturalist. You can inspect those partnerships to decide whether they match the work you want to support.

    Industry observers note that availability varies by country. During this review, a U.S. capture showed the search homepage, while a visit from another region displayed a notice that KARMA was unavailable there and would redirect searches to Bing. Check local availability before making it your default; a regional restriction does not mean the service has closed.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 155,800 to yep.com, October 2026.

    Yep is an Ahrefs-built alternative with a distinctive audience beyond people typing into a search box: developers who want web results for an AI agent or research application. Ahrefs’ current Yep product page describes a first-party crawler, index, and ranking system, with result excerpts and filters for the information an application retrieves.

    Industry observers note that the public search interface captured for this review also returned conventional web results. For an everyday user, that makes it another index to compare; for a developer, the API is the clearer reason to investigate it. The current homepage emphasizes that developer-facing use rather than presenting a Google-like consumer pitch.

    SEJ’s 2022 Yep interview explains the original proposal to share advertising revenue with creators. Although, the current homepage does not establish that those proposed payouts are operating, so they should not be the reason you choose it today.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.4 billion to x.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    In a recent development, x.com is useful when the thing you need is a public statement or conversation: what an organization declared, what a named person said, or how a developing event is being discussed. You are searching posts on the platform, not a general index of webpages.

    That direct access to posted statements is its advantage for news monitoring and research. Its advanced search is a further option for signed-in consumers; the public Explore route redirected to a sign-in screen during this review.

    It has been revealed that use posts to locate leads and original statements, not as automatic confirmation of a claim. Check the account, timestamp, and supporting evidence, especially when an old post is circulating as if it describes a latest event.

    It has been revealed that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 2.1 billion to linkedin.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    LinkedIn is useful when your search starts with a professional identity, such as a person, employer, role, or job. It can also help you find practitioners discussing a work-related subject, rather than only the publishers ranking for that subject on the open web.

    The advantage is the professional context. A name alongside an employer and career history gives you a way to distinguish people who share a name and identify a relevant source. Its public people search is one starting point, although fuller profiles and other features can require signing in.

    Sources indicate that treat profiles as self-reported information, not a verified manufacturer directory. Check current roles and dates against the person’s or organization’s own website when those details matter to your research.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 46.4 million to web.archive.org, October 2026.

    The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine answers a question a current search result often cannot: What did this webpage say before it changed or disappeared? It is useful for checking an old product claim, recovering a removed reference, or following the history of a website.

    It has been revealed that enter the URL and inspect the available captures. The advantage is the dated record where you can compare versions rather than relying on a current page to explain its own past. Check the capture date and whether images and other resources were preserved.

    Sources indicate that the Wayback Machine is part of the wider Internet Archive, whose books, recordings, software, and other collections are separate resources. It is not a complete archive of every page, and a captured claim is evidence of what a page remarked then, not proof that the claim was true.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 39.3 million to slideshare.net, October 2026.

    Industry observers note that slideShare is worth trying when you want the presentation itself, not another article summarizing the subject. A conference talk, research deck, or business pitch can reveal how someone structures an argument and illustrates the details.

    The current homepage describes a collection of more than 25 million presentations. Browsing, reading, and uploading do not require a subscription, while features such as downloading presentations are paid benefits. The value is a format-specific collection you can explore for research or presentation inspiration.

    It has been revealed that check the uploader and publication date before relying on a deck’s statistics or recommendations. Being able to view a presentation also does not automatically give you permission to reuse its artwork.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.1 million to wolframalpha.com, October 2026.

    It has been revealed that wolframAlpha is for questions that need computation rather than a list of pages. If you want to solve an equation, convert units, or work with structured facts, it can calculate an answer from its data and algorithms instead of leaving you to find a suitable calculator elsewhere.

    In a recent development, its explanation of the service describes dynamic computation over curated knowledge. The mathematics examples show the inputs it understands; other areas include science, dates, and measures.

    It has been revealed that that is a different job from comparing recent reporting or finding an opinion. Use it when the result should be computed, and check how it interpreted your units, assumptions, and wording before relying on the output.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 296,200 to openverse.org, October 2026.

    In a recent development, openverse is the tool to try when finding a usable image or audio track matters more than finding a webpage about one. It focuses on openly licensed and public-domain media, making it useful for an article, presentation, or other creative project.

    It has been revealed that its About page describes a collection of more than 800 million images and audio tracks gathered from multiple repositories, with features such as one-click attribution. That collection size is separate from its website traffic. Its advantage is bringing reuse-oriented discovery into one place, rather than treating every image on the web as equally available to use.

    Openly licensed does not mean free of conditions. Licenses can require attribution or restrict commercial use, and Openverse does not verify every work’s licensing information. Follow through to the original source and confirm the license before using a file.

    Recent findings suggest that the introduction of ChatGPT helped bring conversational interfaces into everyday use. In January 2023, SEJ reported that Google’s founders had responded by returning to discussions about its AI response and then opened access to Bard in March 2023.

    It has been revealed that google rolled out AI Overviews to U.S. users in May 2024 and announced AI Mode in 2025. Those developments explain why many services in this list now combine web results with AI generated answers. The two formats can help with different parts of the same research task.

    According to recent reports, google may be the most familiar option, but the best choice for a particular task can be different. Try a few real queries on two or three services, compare the sources, the ease of finding the original information, and the controls you will actually use.

    You can keep one engine for everyday searches and use another for a specific job. A calculation, an archived webpage, and a professional profile do not need to start in the same search box.

    Featured Image: Igor Link/Shutterstock.

    According to recent reports, open your browser’s search settings and choose a supported default engine. If the service is not listed, use its official browser setup instructions. You can also visit its website directly without changing your default.

    Sources indicate that start with the task you want to improve. Try Bing for general web search, DuckDuckGo for a search service centered on privacy, Brave Search for another independent index, and ChatGPT or Perplexity for conversational answers. Compare their results on queries you already know well.

    Some do. Startpage identifies Google and Bing as partners. DuckDuckGo largely sources traditional links and images from Bing. Kagi combines its own indexes with several providers. Brave Search builds an independent web index.

    According to recent reports, no. DuckDuckGo says it is an independent organization. A search provider relationship is different from ownership, and its traditional links and images largely come from Bing.

    Sources indicate that no search tool can guarantee a neutral view of everything online. Index coverage, ranking rules, filters, location, and the query itself affect what appears. Compare independent sources and more than one search engine when the differences matter.

    Business models vary. Some display search advertising, some charge subscriptions, and some combine free and paid services. Read the specific service’s policy because a privacy claim does not mean every product, advertisement, and linked website handles data in the same way.

    Industry News: Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • A latest study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    A latest study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one significant takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    In a recent development, A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less notable — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    In a recent development, that truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    Industry observers note that participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty new. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a substantial gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    According to recent reports, “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, liveKit is the default infrastructure layer for real-time AI — the platform that gives AI the ability to see, hear, and speak. From powering voice for millions of ChatGPT users to enabling drone teleoperation at Skydio and serving as the backbone for roughly 25% of 911 emergency calls in the U.S., LiveKit handles the real-time media layer that production AI applications depend on.

    Industry observers note that over 300,000 developers and 5,000+ companies — from leading AI labs to Fortune 500 enterprises — run production workloads on LiveKit. We've raised $181M from investors including Index Ventures, Altimeter Capital, and Salesforce Ventures, and we're growing fast.

    Our product is deeply technical, and we sell into a brand-newly introduced category: voice AI infrastructure. As we grow our Sales team, our AEs, SDRs, and presales engineers need to understand how LiveKit works, and why real-time voice AI is hard, well enough to hold their own in a customer conversation.

    It has been revealed that we're hiring a Technical Enablement Engineer to own that. You'll build our technical training program from scratch, so ramp time doesn't depend on pulling engineers off the roadmap. You'll sit on the Sales team, report to our CRO, and have a direct line to the engineers building the product.

    This is a hands-on, builder-first enablement role. You'll see the impact of your work directly in how fast newly introduced sellers ramp and how confident they are in front of customers.

    are known as the go-to person for tackling tough technical problems.

    can clearly explain complex technical concepts to people who aren't engineers.

    are a fast learner, frequently picking up fresh languages and tools.

    The best way to impress us is to build something with LiveKit and show us how you'd teach it to someone who has never touched it.

    Audit what AEs, SDRs, and presales know today and where deals stall on technical gaps.

    Build the core curriculum: LiveKit fundamentals, voice AI architecture, agents, and the competitive landscape.

    Ship hands-on labs and sandboxes so sellers build something real, not just watch slides.

    Run technical onboarding for new AEs and SDRs, and create a clear technical learning path for presales and Solutions Architects.

    Certify demo and discovery readiness through hands-on exercises.

    Keep technical content current with every product release, working directly with engineering and product.

    Measure what matters: ramp time, time to first qualified technical conversation, assessment pass rates, and seller confidence.

    A senior-level engineer or technical founder who has shipped production software.

    You've taught or enabled technical content to non-engineers (sales, SEs, or customers) and have a track record to show for it.

    You can explain complex technical concepts simply, to any audience.

    You're a fast learner who ramps quickly on upcoming technology.

    Experience with voice AI, WebRTC, real-time systems, or LLM applications.

    Built a curriculum, bootcamp, or certification program.

    Ran SE or AE onboarding at a dev-tools or infrastructure company.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    • As Senior Accounting Manager, you’ll play a key role in strengthening the financial operations behind that work: owning critical close and technical accounting activities, supporting international entities and audit readiness, and partnering across Finance, Technology, and the business.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LaunchDarkly is building the runtime control layer for the AI era, helping engineering teams govern what ships in production and how software and AI agents behave after deployment.

    As Senior Accounting Manager, you’ll play a key role in strengthening the financial operations behind that work: owning critical close and technical accounting activities, supporting international entities and audit readiness, and partnering across Finance, Technology, and the business. You’ll also lead and develop a global team while improving accounting workflows, systems, and controls, including through automation and AI. This is an opportunity to combine hands-on accounting expertise with meaningful leadership and operational impact at a organization shaping how teams build and run software.

    Target pay ranges based on Geographic Zones* for Level M3:.

    LaunchDarkly operates from a place of high trust and transparency; we are happy to state the pay range for our open roles to best align with your needs. Exact compensation may vary based on skills, experience, and location.

    *Within the United States, our geographic pay zones are defined by counties surrounding major metropolitan areas.**Restricted Stock Units (RSUs), health, vision, and dental insurance, and mental health benefits in addition to salary.

    Industry observers note that modern software delivery was supposed to be the foundation for a thriving digital business but reality has proven otherwise. Slow, inefficient development cycles, costly outages, and fragmented customer experiences are preventing developers from building their best software.     Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries stated they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    In a recent development, for our newly introduced report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Sources indicate that many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries remarked they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    Industry observers note that our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more promptly.

    It has been revealed that “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) remarked they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    It has been revealed that we looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    According to recent reports, using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    According to recent reports, many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) remarked they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    In a recent development, as AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    According to recent reports, as in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    Sources indicate that people across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several crucial questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    It has been revealed that first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    According to recent reports, second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also highlights that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily people and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    #78168. Breaking: AI Citations: What To Check Before Reacting To A Lost One via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2046 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: AI Citations: What To Check Before Reacting To A Lost One via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Around three in four AI citation drops were temporary, according to Ahrefs’ study of the changes in five different AI products over 20 days.
    • When sharing AI citation analysis results with clients or bosses, you should be aware that a loss may not represent what it seems like at first glance.
    • According to recent reports, ahrefs studied about 37,500 first-day citations made by Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews, along with ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around three in four AI citation drops were temporary, according to Ahrefs’ study of the changes in five different AI products over 20 days.

    When sharing AI citation analysis results with clients or bosses, you should be aware that a loss may not represent what it seems like at first glance. Sites in the study that had been cited in answers but then dropped out of those answers were more likely to have another citation occur for them as opposed to staying missing. If someone rewrote a page in the meantime, that rewrite could receive credit for a citation it didn’t earn.

    According to recent reports, ahrefs studied about 37,500 first-day citations made by Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews, along with ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot. The study included only one organization’s view based on its own group of questions answered daily by each tool for 20 days.

    The study’s findings point to four items to look into before making an edit to a webpage based upon the disappearance of a citation.

    Tracking the same citations for consecutive days, the study was able to see what can happen after a site has disappeared from an answer.

    Recent findings suggest that these results were documented by Mateusz Makosiewicz, an SEO and marketing educator at Ahrefs. His colleague Xibeijia Guan collected all websites that had been cited on day one, then traced each reference through to day 20.

    Industry observers note that by day two, about half of those references were gone from AI Overviews. Even more were gone on each of the other tools. Most of these returned prior to the conclusion of the study.

    Across the five tools, about half of the citations that dropped out came back within three days, Ahrefs found.

    The data collected in this study reflects the number of websites, thus when a website comes back, this study cannot determine whether the exact same webpage came back as well.

    Another measure was taken (in Brand Radar’s own tracking of citations), revealing a somewhat comparable pattern with lower rates of return. About two-thirds of all the citations that disappeared from view there ultimately did come back. Ahrefs sells Brand Radar, and the write-up has a section on using it.

    Earlier research I have discussed demonstrated changes in AI responses over multiple runs of a prompt, and this current study adds what happens across different days.

    According to recent reports, I reported on SparkToro’s findings in January regarding their discovery that both ChatGPT and Google’s AI in Search provided the same list of brands less than 1% of the time across repeated runs of the same prompt. They also found that the frequency with which a brand appeared throughout multiple runs was generally more stable than the specific ranking of that brand within those lists.

    According to recent reports, the new study’s authors recommend counting how many of the last seven days a site was cited. This is a frequency count by day for the sites that were cited and the research in January favored a frequency count by run for brand names.

    When a loss occurred on Gemini or Copilot, it often meant there was no one cited at all in the response.

    Industry observers note that gemini had responses without citations about 64% of the time in the data from this study, while Copilot demonstrated answers without citations around 53% of the time. Without citations in an answer, a site will appear as a loss when you track your results.

    Many of the comebacks on those two tools were the tool citing sources again after an answer that cited none. With the empty answers left out, Gemini and Copilot looked much like AI Mode and ChatGPT.

    AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT almost always cited sources. Fewer than 1% of their answers had no citations, and Makosiewicz wrote that a lost citation on those tools almost always means another site took the spot.

    Industry observers note that the first way to verify a lost citation is by looking at the answer. If the answer has no link then you are getting information about the AI tool that day, while if the answer links to a competitor then you have found the site that was cited in your place.

    On Gemini and Copilot, per the write-up, you should keep track of two metrics, the number of times your site gets cited, as well as the frequency with which references are made to another source instead.

    Citations that had stayed active longer before going away were more likely to come back.

    The study ranked all citations on three of the tools (AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT) in order of how long they had been there until they went away the first time.

    For those with a short life span (one day), 34% to 41% of the citations did not return during the study period.

    And for those that remained there for eight to 14 days, this percentage was at or below 4%.

    In a recent development, this suggests that a citation’s history may be more notable than where it stands on a given day. A site referenced once that then disappears is an entirely different circumstance than a site that has maintained its position for 10 days and disappeared yesterday.

    An analysis of occasional check-in reports shows if a site was cited on a specific date (so every site with only one appearance looks like every other site with continuous appearances). Using a seven-day count allows a team to make a distinction. It counts, for each question being asked, the number of days out of the last seven the site was a source referenced. This shows how often a site turns up. How long one citation held is a separate question.

    This process also provides a team with an ongoing assessment of whether an AI tool is consistently relying on a given site to answer those questions.

    Similarly, it can be applied to newly introduced citations. In terms of evaluating the usefulness of a new citation as a lasting win, Makosiewicz suggests waiting a few days before declaring victory. His general rule is to view one missing citation as no reason to change a page, but to review the page if the citation is still missing after two or three weeks.

    A brand can still be named in an answer even after the link to its site disappears.

    In a recent development, A citation is a link readers can follow. A mention is a brand name in the answer text, whether or not it includes a link.

    Each tool used saw approximately 50% to 70% of all cited sites appear on only one day, as opposed to around one in five of all brands named.

    It has been revealed that then your report can display a lost citation while the answer still names the company. The link is still absent, and it still counts as a lost citation, and looking at the answer will tell you which measure has changed.

    Sources indicate that also, AI tools use different versions (longer or shorter) of the same brand name from answer to answer. And a mention that seems to be gone could be the same firm referred to by a different name, so the write-up advises checking for this before subtracting it from your mention totals.

    Since the data highlighted brand names were not moving nearly as much as citations, Makosiewicz suggests that mentions may be the better metric to follow.

    On AI Overviews and AI Mode, pages that also ranked in Google Search for the same question kept their citations longer.

    It has been revealed that in this portion of the study, the authors examined pages. They compared cited pages that appeared somewhere within Google’s results for a question versus those that did not appear anywhere in Google’s results for the same question. On AI Overviews and AI Mode, cited pages that ranked had greater longevity of citation, more often lasting a week or longer; however, the difference between them was smaller for ChatGPT.

    According to recent reports, although appearing in Google’s search results at all correlated with longer-lasting citations more than a page’s exact position in the results list did, according to the write-up, this finding was based on an examination of 230 questions. That comparison showed a correlation between whether pages rank in Google searches for each question and how long the citations to these pages last. Ranking wasn’t a requirement, though. Most of the pages AI Mode and ChatGPT cited didn’t rank in Google for the question they were cited on.

    When a citation stays missing, the authors suggest examining two items, how the page performs in Google Search for the question and how well the page answers the question.

    In September, I proposed a related item to be examined when citations drop while rankings hold steady. That item is to examine the pages being cited in lieu of those originally cited.

    The methodology of this examination also relates to the work performed by SEO teams. When a page loses its Google ranking for a particular question and subsequently drops off of the AI Overview citations, looking into why the page lost its ranking would be a logical starting point to investigate.

    Most citations that disappeared came back during the study, so one comeback alone may not be strong evidence that a page change caused it.

    A team that edits a page after losing a citation and then sees the citation come back has two explanations for it. An edit can’t be credited as working (it may have been due to some other reason) when there is only one comeback to support this.

    Makosiewicz wrote, “Don’t credit a page edit for a single comeback.”.

    In essence, he wants us to look at an increase in the number of times a site reference appears over a longer time span.

    In addition, it would be weak evidence that an edit damaged a citation when that citation disappears the very next day after you edit a page, because half or more of citations disappeared by the next day in the study.

    According to recent reports, A number of things can be checked by someone before they change the page behind a lost citation. First, they can look again over the next several days to see whether the citation is still missing. Second, they can read the response itself.

    Management will learn a lot more from a count like five of the last seven, when an in-house team reports how many days a site was cited, than from simply receiving a yes or no from one check.

    An agency has an order to follow on a client call, checking the text of the response, the history of the citation and the ranking of the page prior to making a proposal for latest content.

    A content team will get a warning about correlation vs. causation. One comeback after an edit does not provide you with sufficient evidence to make similar edits to other pages.

    The researchers measured the disappearance of citations; they did not test if changing a page brings back a citation that has gone missing.

    In a recent development, they only tracked the very first time a citation went missing. The data collected does not reveal how frequently those same citations disappeared again after returning.

    According to recent reports, the researchers wrote that their figures may represent an underestimate of citations returning as citations that disappeared at the end of the study had less time to return than citations that were lost early in the study. Changes to models could also affect the stability of citation patterns over time.

    Industry observers note that the next lost citation will be much easier to read when you have something to reference already. Having a daily log of which sites are cited, related to the questions that matter most, can help provide your team’s own internal tally of days cited prior to a client or manager asking why citations are down.

    When a citation is still missing after two or three weeks, the study’s advice is to look at the page, beginning with how it ranks for the question.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    In a recent development, as pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and fresh hybrid work schedules.

    Sources indicate that on Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.

    In a recent development, are there any I’m missing? Let me know. And read the full piece here.

    The upcoming budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Industry observers note that expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    Sources indicate that “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan remarked. “They see what Major Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s significant local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a upcoming tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    In a recent development, the labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan noted.

    There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    Sources indicate that “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    It has been revealed that in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    In a recent development, but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Debuted in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    It has been revealed that “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Industry observers note that many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

    Sources indicate that some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    It has been revealed that deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    It has been revealed that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan remarked. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    In a recent development, for a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Industry observers note that revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    In a recent development, LION Publishers stated in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    Sources indicate that LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

    OpenNews remarked in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    It has been revealed that the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    In a recent development, the three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he remarked. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    #78157. A Charity Rescue Dog Outscored Amazon’s Christmas Ad – PPC Accounts Need A Story Before Cyber Week via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
