    • The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old firm is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old firm is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

    Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

    The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

    From the rollout of new lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”.

    A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

    It has been revealed that dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”.

    McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

    Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”.

    Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”.

    According to recent reports, little discussed, however, were the manufacturer’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, said that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”.

    According to recent reports, “Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred noted. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”.

    The meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

    “There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter said. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the company can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”.

    For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by Upcoming Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

    In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

    Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

    Many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “company-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

    Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, said earlier this month.

    It has been revealed that “In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant mentioned. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”.

    It has been revealed that trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

    Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”.

    Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”.

    “They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” mentioned the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

    It has been revealed that readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH.

    — James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026.

    Industry observers note that given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter mentioned, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

    “It is important that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter mentioned. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a latest model to help customers make better decisions.”.

    In a recent development, in recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection organization Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building new audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, mentioned Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

    Such a reality is already playing out in Washington, remarked Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the company’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”.

    “We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred remarked. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”.

    Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its latest AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

    A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “tech giant’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”.

    “From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch fresh brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”.

    The insights into the company’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

    “The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred noted. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”.

    Sources indicate that hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he stated, the organization seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

    Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

    “We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch said during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a new movie, a new book, a new product.”.

    Building fresh audiences is critical as the manufacturer works to claw itself out of debt, remarked Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

    In a recent development, “Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri mentioned. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”.

    Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

    It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”.

    Sources indicate that you may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

    Sources indicate that but with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something fresh?

    These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out looks. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a fresh white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:.

    In a recent development, taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely new kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams massive!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization.

    De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters.

    In a recent development, pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year.     By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:.

    Recent findings suggest that endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities.     This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    Recent findings suggest that and for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

    Sources indicate that pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

    Sources indicate that I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous new rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

    But the upcoming Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for massive dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    According to recent reports, our Sales team needs a dedicated data partner, and creator commerce (how creators monetize by selling digital products) is becoming a bigger part of how Kit and our creators scale. Kit is growing, so we're looking for a Senior Analytics Engineer to own Kit's sales and commerce data from end to end.

    It has been revealed that accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions. That’s what makes this role so important.

    Industry observers note that your primary focus will be Sales: the dbt models that turn our CRM data into trusted pipeline, deal, and funnel metrics, and the Omni dashboards our sales leader and Senior Revenue Operations Manager use to run the business. You'll also model creator commerce data, so we understand what creators sell and earn through Kit, and you'll pick up reporting work with our Product team, such as feature usage reporting. On a small data team, we step outside our usual lanes when the need is there, so the mix will shift over time.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll build for two kinds of consumers: people and AI. Teammates increasingly answer their own questions by querying our semantic layer through Omni's AI and MCP connections to AI tools. That means your models, metric definitions, and documentation need to be clear and correct enough for an AI agent to use them without a data teammate in the loop.

    According to recent reports, this is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes being close to the business, enjoys turning messy operational data into numbers people trust, and is happy to work on both the models and the dashboards that sit on top of them. When Sales and Product have clear, reliable data, we help more creators build more valuable businesses with Kit.

    You'll report to Sam Umachi, Head of Data (Linkedin).

    Sales and RevOps are your primary partners, who will rely on the models and reporting you own. You'll also partner with our Product team on reporting for features like Visual Automations and on how creators use Kit.

    According to recent reports, within our data team, you'll work alongside a Staff Analytics Engineer who owns org-wide semantic layer governance and modeling standards, a Senior Data Engineer who owns ingestion and pipelines, and a Senior Business Analytics Partner focused on revenue opportunities. This role has no direct reports.

    Sources indicate that first Week: Work through our onboarding curriculum in Notion and meet the data team, our Senior Revenue Operations Manager, the sales team, and your product partners. Get set up in our core tools: dbt Cloud, GitHub, Amazon Redshift, Omni, HubSpot, Linear, Hightouch and Slack. Set up your AI-assisted development environment and learn the shared AI workflows our data team uses. Open and merge your first small pull request so you learn our review and deployment flow early.

    First Month: Map how HubSpot objects (deals, pipelines and stages, companies, contacts, and owners) flow into our dbt models, and document the gaps. Take over day-to-day ownership of the sales models and Omni dashboards that teammates have been covering. Audit current sales reporting and list where definitions differ or numbers don't reconcile. Get familiar with how commerce data (products creators sell and the revenue they earn through Kit) lands in the warehouse today. Agree with RevOps and Sales on the most key questions they need answered. Review teammates' pull requests and contribute to our shared SQL, dbt, and documentation standards. Share a written reflection with the team on what you've learned and where you'd focus first.

    First Six Months: Ship and maintain well-tested, documented dbt models for core sales metrics, such as pipeline, deal velocity, stage conversion, win rates, and the sales-led funnel. Expose those metrics through the Omni semantic layer, working within the team's governance standards. Rebuild or refresh the core sales dashboards so pipeline reviews and forecasting conversations run on numbers that don't need manual reconciliation. Resolve competing sales metric definitions by writing down the options and tradeoffs, aligning with Sales and RevOps, and documenting the outcome. Model creator-level commerce data, such as products sold, revenue earned through Kit, and conversion, in partnership with data engineering. Write semantic layer descriptions, metric definitions, and documentation that let Omni's AI and MCP-connected AI tools answer routine sales questions correctly, and test them against real questions from Sales, RevOps and Product. Get Sales to the point where routine questions are answered through self-serve, whether in Omni dashboards, Omni's AI, or AI tools connected over MCP, rather than one-off requests.

    According to recent reports, first Year: Be the recognized owner of Kit's sales data, the person Sales and RevOps go to first and trust without second-guessing. Give our revenue analysis work the sales and commerce models it depends on, so deeper questions about pipeline health and creator earnings can be answered rapidly, thereby enabling us to make creators more successful. Leave your domains well documented and well tested, legible to latest teammates, stakeholders, and the AI agents that query our semantic layer. Help raise the team's modeling quality through code review, pairing, and sharing what you learn.

    In a recent development, deep dbt experience. You build modular, tested, documented dbt projects, and you're comfortable with incremental models, snapshots, macros, CI, and scheduled jobs in dbt Cloud or similar.

    Advanced SQL. You reason carefully about grain, joins, and window functions, and you write queries that are readable and performant on a cloud warehouse.

    Recent findings suggest that data modeling for sales and GTM. You can model deals, pipeline stages and their history, ownership changes, and funnel conversion into clean, reusable structures. You are opinionated on Kimball standards and when a concept should be a fact or dimension.

    In a recent development, CRM data fluency. You know how sales data behaves in a CRM, including stage changes, backdated edits, and custom properties. HubSpot is preferred, but other CRM experience (e.g. Salesforce) applies just as well. We care most that you recognize common CRM patterns.

    AI-assisted development. You use AI code editors and agents (such as Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, or similar) every day, and you validate their output with tests, query results, and review before anything ships.

    Recent findings suggest that clear written communication. You explain metric definitions, tradeoffs, and data caveats in plain language that Sales, RevOps, and Product partners understand.

    BI and semantic layer experience. You can build dashboards and semantic models in Omni, Looker, or a similar BI tool, and you design metric definitions that people and AI tools can both query correctly.

    Git-based workflows. You keep pull requests small and well described, and you give thoughtful code review.

    Nice to have: Redshift performance tuning (sort and distribution keys), Python for scripting or API pulls, reverse ETL, and experience with product event, billing, payments, or ecommerce data.

    Around 7 or more years in analytics engineering or data engineering where you personally shipped production data models.

    Several years of hands-on work building and maintaining production dbt projects.

    Working directly with sales teams and RevOps, and owning reporting they relied on to run the business.

    Owning a data domain over time and evolving its models as the business and its questions changed.

    Sources indicate that working at a SaaS firm, ideally one with both a self-serve and a sales-led motion. Commerce, payments, or creator economy experience is a plus, not a requirement.

    Working on a small or remote team where you were trusted to make decisions independently.

    Recent findings suggest that ownership and follow-through. You treat your data domains as yours. You notice problems before stakeholders do, close the loop on requests, and finish what you start.

    Judgment. You match rigor to the decision at hand, know when a quick answer is enough and when a request should become a durable model, and say so clearly.

    Industry observers note that flexibility. You're glad to step outside your primary area when another team needs help, and you balance that work against your core commitments openly.

    In a recent development, teach everything you know. You document as you go, pair generously, and help stakeholders understand the data well enough to use it on their own.

    Work in public. You share progress, open questions, and decisions in writing where the team can see them, including what didn't work.

    Creator success is our success. You remember who's on the other end. A wrong number in a pipeline review means Sales spends time on the wrong creators, and that shapes how carefully you work.

    Do it with excellence. You test your work, review it carefully, and don't ship a number you can't defend.

    Industry observers note that candor with care. You're comfortable pushing back when a request won't answer the real question, and you do it in a way that builds trust.

    Needing detailed specs or a highly structured environment before you can start.

    In a recent development, discomfort with ambiguity. Some of our sales and commerce definitions are still evolving, and you'll help settle them.

    Needing several layers of approval to make modeling decisions within your domain.

    Wanting to work only on dashboards, or only on pipelines, rather than across the transformation and BI layers.

    According to recent reports, wanting a strictly fixed scope. Sales comes first, but you'll pick up Product or other work when the business needs it.

    Wanting mostly greenfield work. Much of this role is improving sales models and dashboards that already exist.

    Preferring to take tickets as written rather than partnering with stakeholders on what they need.

    Being skeptical of AI's capabilities, or using AI without good judgment and accountability.

    Expecting a large data team with dedicated specialists for every part of the stack.

    Industry observers note that we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Sources indicate that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at our level 4 ($172,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    Industry observers note that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Tech giant-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a organization is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.”.

    Industry observers note that benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase. The post further states, “No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics,” and then pitches Palmata as a tool that monitors what AI assistants say about a business, offers recommendations on what changes need to be made, and simulates the effect of those changes prior to publication.

    Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.

    In a recent development, salesforce’s guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) says SEO “isn’t going away” and that “SEO is still the foundation.” Graham Hardt, whose byline lists him as SEO Senior Director, wrote it for fresh businesses, and Salesforce published it Sept. 11. Palmata’s product page links to the guide from its FAQ.

    Sources indicate that contentful introduced Palmata in June; it became a part of Salesforce when Salesforce’s acquisition of Contentful occurred on Sept. 1. The article announcing the launch of Palmata, written by Jason McGhee, head of product and engineering for Palmata, said that SEO gave organizations “a practical framework for improving visibility” and added, “That work remains essential.”.

    Aleyda Solis, an SEO and AI search consultant who founded Orainti, wrote in a quote post that AI search “relies on many of the same fundamentals as SEO.” Her post continues, “AI search optimization goes beyond traditional SEO, but it certainly doesn’t replace it.”.

    Solis also wrote that measuring AI search visibility matters, “but monitoring what AI platforms say about your brand and actually improving your visibility, recommendations and business outcomes are very different things.”.

    Pedro Dias, a technical SEO product manager who used to work at Google, wrote that SEO “was never a topic that attracted the interest of decision makers.” His post adds, “SEO isn’t traffic. It never has been.”.

    Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic, replied to Benioff, “This gold rush already happened and the market is already oversaturated.” Growth advisor Eli Schwartz wrote that “there’s yet another AEO tool in the mix.”.

    When Benioff’s post is read by a marketing executive, Salesforce’s own guide answers it, stating that SEO and AEO are “two visibility layers for the same audience.”.

    In terms of making the case for fresh businesses to include both SEO and AEO, this guide provides Salesforce’s reasoning for including SEO in your looks right alongside any AI visibility tool, such as Palmata.

    According to Palmata’s FAQ section, Palmata is a standalone tool that is also built into Marketing Cloud by Salesforce. In weighing tools like Palmata, Salesforce’s guide states you should track “both sets of metrics.” This means tracking your organic traffic and rankings, but also tracking how many times you’ve been cited by AI.

    • Stations in Latest Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Stations in Latest Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    In a recent development, more than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Newly introduced Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    Recent findings suggest that like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, noted NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also key to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Counterpart is the first Agentic Insurance™ platform, combining trusted insurance expertise with cutting-edge AI to deliver tailored management and professional liability solutions. By integrating Agentic Underwriting™, Agentic Broker Services™, Agentic Risk Mitigation™, Agentic Claims Management™, Agentic Coverage™, and Agentic Capacity™ into one powerful platform, Counterpart empowers brokers - and the businesses they serve - to do more with less risk. Backed by A rated carriers, Counterpart has been recognized by CB Insights as a 2025 “Top 50 Insurtech,” by Great Place to Work, and by Business Insurance as one of its 2025 “Best Places to Work.”.

    Industry observers note that as Senior Accountant, you execute the day-to-day financial operations within Agentic Finance - premium accounts receivable and cash application, accounts payable, bank and balance sheet reconciliations, bordereau and premium reconciliation, carrier and claims payments, expense management, and audit and tax support - that keep Counterpart, Agentic Programs™, and Counterpart Insurance Tech giant running. You support premium cash application, accounts payable, bank reconciliations, expense management, and vendor administration, and you prepare the bordereau, carrier payment, close, and audit work that the Accounting Manager and Controller review. You build and use the agents that make this execution more efficient as the company scales. You report to the Controller and work closely with the Accounting Manager.

    Industry observers note that our estimated pay range for this role is $110,000 to $130,000. Base salary is determined by a variety of factors, including but not limited to, market data, location, internal equitability, and experience.

    It has been revealed that we are committed to being a welcoming and inclusive workplace for everyone, and we are intentional about making sure people feel respected, supported and connected at work - regardless of who you are or where you come from. We value and celebrate our differences and we believe being open about who we are allows us to do the best work of our lives.

    It has been revealed that we are an Equal Opportunity Employer.     From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

    It has been revealed that it’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

    The Chicago Sun-Times revealed a newly introduced slogan this week. What is it?

    “Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

    An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this company voted this week to authorize a strike.

    “The union has been negotiating a fresh contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”.

    According to recent reports, A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

    The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

    A major journalism school announced this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

    Sources indicate that “Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for New Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”.

    At this week’s summit in China, Bloomberg TV reporter Annmarie Hordern asked Donald Trump whether he felt Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. What happened next?

    “It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”.

    Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

    Unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

    This is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

    With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a big increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

    YouTube has found a latest way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

    “YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also notes the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching highlights.”.

    In Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

    Since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government plans to scrap public media license fees.

    • According to recent reports, wordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, fresh data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.

    WordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API. Google also published the referrer values its traffic sends and shared ways in which a CDN move could lead to blocking Googlebot. Ask Maps began contacting local businesses, and United Airlines included its AI agent rules within its terms.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    According to recent reports, wordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec. 8, contains a new feature called /random/, turned on by default, to send a visitor to a randomly selected published post. There is no option in the dashboard settings for this to be turned off.

    According to recent reports, key facts: According to the developer note, /random/ randomly selects posts and also custom post types as long as they are publicly queryable and have archives (unless the developer has registered them using 'randomable' => false) and excludes pages and attachments. The development code uses a 302 status code along with an X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow HTTP header when it redirects the visitor but does not send that header on the post that the visitor arrives at. To turn the feature off, developers need the wp_enable_random_content_redirect filter, and the different spelling given in WordPress’s November developer news roundup isn’t found anywhere in the code.

    In a recent development, testimonials for clients (and other custom post type entries) may never be accessed via navigation. When their post type is eligible, they can be reached through /random/, even if they have been set to noindex by an SEO plugin. Before you update, check which post types would meet WordPress’s eligibility criteria, and ask a developer to exclude those that should not show up.

    Read our full coverage: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made.

    Teams using the Search Console API can now segment the data they pull into branded and non-branded searches without having to maintain a list of their brands as regular expressions (regex).

    Key facts: Three Performance report features were added to the Search Analytics API by Google on Nov. 16. The brandedClassification dimension works only with eligible properties, and according to the API reference, the data provided for this dimension starts on Feb. 21, 2026. Setting type to webMultimodal returns results from Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android and image uploads, and a fresh filterLists field allows you to filter by multiple countries or devices in a single request.

    It has been revealed that for reports covering dates before Feb. 21, 2026, you’ll still need your own brand regex. Google’s announcement of the branded queries filter claims “some queries may occasionally be misidentified,” so comparing the API split with the regex you already use can help you spot where they differ.

    Read our full coverage: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    A google.com referrer lets you know in your analytics when Google sends a visitor, but it doesn’t show which source (Search, Discover or Google Images) was behind it, notes a newly introduced Search Central page.

    Key facts: The page was listed Nov. 12 in Google’s documentation updates log. It says Google Search utilizes an origin referrer policy for its Search results; thus, the header will contain only the scheme and host, and not the search query. Referrers from Discover carry the values of the surface where Discover was viewed. Same-origin services such as Google Images send the same values as Search and Discover.

    To distinguish Discover clicks from Search clicks, use Search Console’s Discover report rather than referrer data. If Google traffic appears as referral or direct in your analytics, Google’s page recommends checking whether custom channel rules, referral exclusions, or filters are reclassifying it.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Find Search Traffic In Analytics & Logs.

    A CDN can let Googlebot crawl your site faster before the CDN’s cache has filled, according to Google, and those requests then go to your origin server.

    Recent findings suggest that key facts: On Nov. 11, Search Central posted Google’s explanation that a fast and reliable CDN may slowly increase a site’s crawl capacity limit, while a brand upcoming CDN begins with an empty cache. The first visit to each URL is a cache miss, so the page has to come from your origin server, and crawlers visit far more of your site’s URLs than visitors do, with most visitors sticking to a small set of popular pages. When admins block all bots from their site using blanket bot protection, they can cause Googlebot to fail CAPTCHA challenges. If this stays in place, then the pages of the site begin to drop out of search results.

    Recent findings suggest that google’s advice for the move is to allow verified bots in the CDN and firewall settings, then pre-warm caches by fetching your most popular and frequently crawled URLs before switching traffic. Before enabling bot protection during the migration, be sure the verified-bot setting is turned on.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems.

    According to recent reports, google’s Ask Maps has started calling some U.S. beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses to identify available appointment times for customers.

    According to recent reports, key facts: On Nov. 16 a post from Google said that customers can use Ask Maps to find these appointments online and have it call local businesses, then see available time slots so the customer can decide where to book. The feature started rolling out on Android and iOS, with the ability to find appointments launching in the U.S. first. Google already makes automated calls to businesses for customers using Google Search and Maps, including booking appointments and confirming availability, and this process is covered in Google’s Business Profile help page.

    In Google’s demo, Ask Maps shows four times for a gel manicure that it confirmed were available online.

    It has been revealed that the setting Google documents for those automated calls is the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” option in Advanced settings in your verified Business Profile. However, Google’s Ask Maps post does not indicate if calls received via Ask Maps are subject to this setting. Check what you have set, and make sure whoever answers the phone knows these calls come from Google on behalf of a customer.

    Read our full coverage: Google Adds Appointment Finding & Business Calls To Ask Maps.

    Sources indicate that united Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, let search engines index its public pages but require written permission for any AI agent that searches, books or buys on its site or app.

    It has been revealed that key facts: The terms also bar using data from United’s site or app, such as fares and schedules, to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt named no AI crawlers or agents. Separately, HUMAN Security’s October report found that Meta’s and OpenAI’s agents made about 90% of the agent requests on sites and apps it protects.

    In HUMAN Security’s October data, Muse accounted for 59% of agent requests. Three OpenAI agents accounted for about 30% combined.

    In a recent development, meta’s Muse publishes no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Slobodan Manic wrote in October, so whether it gets in comes down to your terms and bot protection. Muse sent the most requests in HUMAN’s data, and bot rules can check the signatures some of its requests carry, whose key directory DataDome reported had moved to muse.ai by Nov. 9.

    Read our full coverage: United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First and Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data.

    In a recent development, much of this week’s SEO work sits with teams outside of SEO. The next steps for this week include identifying who is responsible for the off switch for the /random/ redirect, as well as reporting on the branded split and the analytics rules for referrers. Google’s CDN advice should be reviewed by whoever runs the CDN and firewall, and the automated calls toggle is managed through the Business Profile. United’s rules related to agents are contained within a legal agreement. Before the next change, the first step is to determine who has responsibility for each of these in your own organization.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    We are hiring a Sr. Manager, Total Rewards to lead the design, delivery, and continuous improvement of Camunda’s global compensation, benefits, and equity programs. This person will partner closely with the People team, Finance, and Legal to make sure our rewards are competitive, equitable, compliant, and easy to understand in every country where we operate. This is a hands-on, strategic role for a rewards leader who wants to build and run programs as a trusted business partner, not just administer them. The right candidate will bring deep technical rewards expertise, strong AI and analytical skills, and a passion for a great employee experience. We also expect this leader to be AI-forward in how we approach compensation strategy and job leveling, not only in how they use AI to get their own work done. That means using AI and data-driven methods to shape pay philosophy, benchmark and model market data, design and calibrate our job architecture and leveling framework, and make faster, more consistent, and more transparent rewards decisions.

    Own the global Total Rewards strategy across compensation, benefits, equity, and recognition, and make sure it helps Camunda attract, retain, and motivate top talent. Set an AI-forward vision for how Camunda designs and runs compensation, and turn it into a practical roadmap.

    Lead the annual compensation cycle, including merit, promotion, and equity planning, in partnership with People Business Partners, Finance, and business leaders.

    Recent findings suggest that own job architecture, leveling, and grading frameworks, and keep the Job Catalog accurate as the company grows. Apply AI and data-driven approaches to job leveling, such as consistent role-to-level mapping, calibration, and level-drift detection, with human oversight.

    Run market benchmarking and compensation analysis, and turn the findings into clear, data-driven recommendations for leadership. Use AI to speed up and improve benchmarking, pay modeling, and scenario analysis.

    Manage benefits programs and vendor relationships across regions, including EOR providers such as Remote.com, brokers, and equity administration platforms, with a clear view of cost, service levels, and employee value.

    Ensure compliance with pay transparency, pay equity, and local compensation and benefits regulations in every jurisdiction where Camunda operates.

    Partner with Finance on compensation budgeting and equity pool management, and track total rewards spend against a clear baseline.

    Advise People Business Partners and hiring managers on offers, pay decisions, and exceptions, balancing internal equity, market data, budget and capturing and retaining strong AI talent..

    Identify and adopt AI and automation tools that improve rewards analytics, benchmarking, and employee communications, and ensure AI use complies with local laws and regulations.

    Lead, coach, and develop the Total Rewards team, setting clear priorities and growth paths.

    Manage Camunda’s Relationship with our EOR.

    Ability and/or willingness to use our product.

    Bachelor’s degree in HR, Finance, Business, or a related field. A CCP, CEBS, or similar certification is a plus.

    8+ years of Total Rewards experience, including significant compensation and benefits experience at a global, multi-country technology or SaaS company.

    Hands-on experience leading a global compensation cycle (merit, promotion, and equity) and running market benchmarking with tools such as Radford, Pave, or similar.

    Experience managing benefits, EOR, and equity vendor relationships, including platforms such as Remote or similar.

    Strong analytical and modeling skills, with the ability to translate complex data into practical, business-pragmatic recommendations.

    Working knowledge of pay transparency, pay equity, and compensation regulations across multiple jurisdictions, ideally including the EU and USA.

    Experience using AI and automation tools to improve rewards analytics and workflows.

    AI-forward approach to compensation strategy and job leveling, with real examples of using AI or advanced analytics to shape pay philosophy, model market data, build or calibrate job architecture and levels, or improve pay decisions, and the judgment to keep humans accountable for fairness, compliance, and explainability.

    Excellent written and verbal communication, with the ability to build trust across People, Finance, and Legal.

    Experience leading or developing a team and influencing senior stakeholders.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    According to recent reports, we offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    The Annual Total Target Cash (base salary + 100% variable target, where applicable) shown below spans from the minimum in a Standard market to the maximum in a Major market. Final offers depend on skills, experience, and location, and we typically hire in the first half of the range to allow room for growth:.

    United Kingdom: £114,900.00 to £189,000.00.

    Singapore: S$227,300.00 to S$340,900.00.

    If you’re based elsewhere, you’ll be hired via Remote.com (our global employer partner), and your Talent Acquisition Partner will provide a personalized Total Rewards Calculator after your first interview.

    Equity: We also offer equity (where applicable) through our Virtual Stock Option Plan (VSOP).

    We invest in your wellbeing, growth, and ability to connect, along with perks that support you no matter where you’re based. Our benefits are globally designed and locally delivered where applicable.

    Remote & Flexible: Work from anywhere with the setup that suits you, home office budget, co-working space support, and flexible time off to recharge when you need it.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.

    Health & Wellbeing: Access locally tailored healthcare, Modern Health for global mental wellbeing, and our Live Well Lifestyle Spending Account (LSA), a flexible, global benefit that puts you in control of your whole life, not just work, from: staying active, to caring for family, exploring personal passions, meaningful experiences, and investing in your financial wellbeing.     Financial Security: Retirement and pension intends (often with company contributions), plus life and disability insurance where relevant.

    Professional Growth: Up to $/€/£1,000 per year for self-driven learning: courses, certifications, books, you decide!

All qualified applicants will receive consideration without regard to gender, race, ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, age, disability or any other protected characteristics under applicable law. We are looking forward to your application!

    We're hiring a Product Manager to own Postgres itself at Supabase. Every Supabase project is a full Postgres database, and Postgres is the foundation that Auth, Storage, Realtime and Edge Functions run on. You'll own the product experience of the database: Postgres versions and upgrades, maintenance, observability, extensions and security.

    You'll work closely with our Postgres engineering teams and with the PM lead for Databases, who leads Multigres. You'll define the Postgres requirements that architecture must meet, and own how customers experience their database through that transition.

    In a recent development, this role is ideal for someone who loves Postgres, sweats the details that make a database trustworthy, and is excited about improving the experience for millions of developers. Small improvements here compound across every project on the platform.

    In a recent development, you'll own Postgres versions, upgrades and end-of-life. Which major and minor versions we support, how and when customers upgrade, and how we retire old versions. Your goal is to make upgrades routine rather than risky.

    In a recent development, you'll make maintenance predictable. You'll design how we schedule, communicate and run maintenance windows so customers stay informed and in control, and disruption is rare and expected.

    Sources indicate that you'll help developers understand their database. Query performance, metrics, logs and advisors: you'll own the path from "my database is slow" to the fix.

    You'll own our extension ecosystem. Which extensions we offer, how we evaluate and support fresh ones, and how we keep them working across versions.

    Industry observers note that you'll own Postgres security. Roles and permissions, Row Level Security ergonomics, secure defaults, and how we respond to Postgres and extension CVEs.

    You'll talk to developers across the full spectrum, from indie developers on their first project to enterprises running critical workloads, and bring what you learn into every prioritization call.

    You'll own the problem definition, requirements and success metrics for what we ship, such as upgrade success rate, the share of the fleet on supported versions, and time-to-diagnose for performance problems. You'll set the metric before the team builds, then track it after launch.

    You'll keep Engineering, Support and GTM aligned. You'll own the initiative of record for what's coming, why, and in what order, and communicate version changes and deprecations clearly to customers.

    Recent findings suggest that 4+ years of Product Management experience on databases, developer tools or infrastructure, or equivalent depth as an engineer, DBA or founder moving into product. You're comfortable commenting on an architecture doc and advocating for the user when trade-offs are required.

    It has been revealed that know Postgres well, or another relational database well enough to ramp quickly. You're comfortable reading EXPLAIN output and talking about replication, WAL, roles and extensions.

    Recent findings suggest that have shipped products where reliability and trust are the experience. You treat downtime and breaking changes as product problems, not just operational ones.

    Recent findings suggest that write clearly. Your specs, announcements and deprecation notices leave little room for confusion.

    Build with what you own. You run queries, test upgrades and try extensions yourself, and form opinions through first-hand use.

    Product Builder at Camunda
